report:
## Vitamin C and the Common Cold: What the Evidence Shows

Your intuition is largely correct, with an important caveat.

**For the general population: No meaningful preventive effect.** The definitive evidence comes from the Cochrane systematic review by Hemilä and Chalker, which pooled data from over 11,000 participants across 29 trial comparisons. Regular daily vitamin C supplementation (typically ≥0.2 g/day) did **not** reduce the incidence (the number of people who catch a cold) in the general population (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/, https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold). This directly contradicts the popular belief popularized by Linus Pauling in the 1970s.

**Modest effects on duration/severity, not prevention.** Regular supplementation was associated with a small but consistent reduction in the *duration* and *severity* of cold symptoms once a cold occurred (about 8% shorter in adults, up to 18% in children at higher doses) — but this is treatment of symptoms, not prevention of catching a cold (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2007/1015/p1111a, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10712193/).

**One notable exception: extreme physical stress.** Five trials (598 participants) involving marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions found vitamin C nearly halved cold incidence (RR ~0.5) in this specific, narrow context of intense short-term physical/cold stress — a subgroup finding that doesn't generalize to typical daily life (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold).

**Bottom line:** For most people, regular vitamin C does not prevent colds. It may modestly shorten colds once they start, and may help prevent colds specifically for people undergoing intense physical exertion — but broad prophylactic use for cold prevention is not supported by high-quality evidence.
